questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a revision changes audience or only style

stimulus.body: Original brief is written for engineers. Revision adds a glossary and simplifies sentences but keeps all technical values.

questions.stem: Does the revision change the audience or only the style?

options.text: It changes the audience to non-experts.
It changes only the style, same audience.
It removes technical content.
It proves the original was wrong.

questions.explanation: A glossary and simplified sentences target non-expert readers. Style changes alone would not need a glossary.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the move of enumerating supporting reasons
questions.stem: In a brief, the phrase 'Three reasons support this choice: cost, durability, and availability' performs which move?

options.text: It enumerates supporting reasons.
It introduces a counterargument.
It retracts the choice.
It defines a single term.

questions.explanation: Listing cost, durability, and availability enumerates support. It is not a counterargument, retraction, or definition.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unsupported generalisation is risky
questions.stem: A brief states 'All our welds are defect-free' with no inspection records; explain the risk.

answer.exemplar: The universal claim lacks inspection evidence, so any later defect can invalidate the whole statement and damage credibility or liability.

questions.explanation: Unsupported universals are fragile. One counter-example collapses the claim and harms trust.
questions.hint: What happens if one defect appears?

options.text: Bury the risk in a footnote.
State the risk in bold at the top.
Remove the risk to avoid alarm.
Replace the risk with a joke.

questions.explanation: Prominent placement highlights risk. Hiding, removing, or trivialising it undermines safety communication.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the move of restating a requirement as a constraint

stimulus.body: The brief notes the client requires 100-year design life, then frames all material choices around that limit.

questions.stem: What move does framing choices around the 100-year limit perform?

options.text: It restates a requirement as a governing constraint.
It rejects the client's requirement.
It shortens the design life.
It proves 100 years is optimal.

questions.explanation: Using the 100-year requirement to govern choices restates it as a constraint. It does not reject, shorten, or prove optimality.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a survey of three peers supports a method claim

stimulus.body: A brief claims a new curing method is superior because three engineers on the team prefer it.

questions.stem: Does the peer survey support the method claim?

options.text: Yes, because expert preference indicates quality.
No, because preference is not performance data.
Yes, because three is a sufficient sample.
No, because engineers are biased.

questions.explanation: Preference does not demonstrate performance. Expertise does not convert opinion into data, and bias claims dodge the evidence issue.
questions.hint: What kind of evidence is preference?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Analyze which counter-example most challenges a universal claim
questions.stem: Which counter-example most challenges the claim 'All our joints pass inspection'?

options.text: A joint that passed with minor notes.
options.misconception: a pass is not a challenge

options.text: A joint that failed inspection last month.
A joint that has not been inspected.
options.misconception: absence of inspection is not a failure

options.text: A joint in a different building.

questions.explanation: A failed joint directly contradicts 'all pass'. Minor notes, uninspected joints, and location do not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the move of softening a recommendation for a cautious board

stimulus.body: Original: 'Replace the bridge now.' Revision: 'Consider scheduling replacement within two years.' The board is cautious and budget-constrained.

questions.stem: What move does the revision perform for the board?

options.text: It softens the recommendation and adds a timeframe.
It strengthens the urgency.
It cancels the replacement.
It blames the board for delay.

questions.explanation: 'Consider scheduling within two years' softens the imperative and adds a timeframe. It does not strengthen, cancel, or blame.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a statistic supports a broad safety claim

stimulus.body: A brief claims the design is safe because 99 percent of similar bridges survived a decade. The sample includes only low-traffic rural bridges.

questions.stem: Does the statistic support the broad safety claim?

options.text: Yes, because 99 percent is very high.
No, because the sample excludes high-traffic cases.
Yes, because a decade is long enough.
No, because statistics are never useful.

questions.explanation: The sample excludes high-traffic bridges, so the statistic does not support a broad claim. High percentage or long duration do not fix the mismatch.
questions.hint: Does the sample match the claim's scope?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a revision preserves meaning while improving flow

stimulus.body: Original: 'The beam is strong. It holds 50 kN. That is enough.' Revision: 'The beam holds 50 kN, which is enough, so it is strong.'

questions.stem: Does the revision preserve meaning while improving flow?

options.text: Yes, it merges sentences without changing meaning.
No, it changes meaning by adding 'so'.
No, it removes the 50 kN figure.
Yes, but only because it is shorter.

questions.explanation: The revision combines sentences and adds 'so', but the proposition is unchanged. The 50 kN figure remains, and flow improves by reducing choppiness.
questions.hint: Check the facts and the connective.
